findings.title: PythOracle Negative Price Wraps to ~1.8e19
findings.description: uint256(uint64(price.price)) casts Pyth's int64 price to uint64. Negative prices (valid in Pyth protocol) wrap to ~1.8e19 instead of reverting. The wrapped value feeds into getExchangeRate() and getMinAmountReceived(), causing all orders using PythOracle to execute at a wildly incorrect price.

findings.title: Bracket performUpkeep: Permissionless with Attacker-Controlled Routing
findings.description: performUpkeep() has no access control. The caller supplies target and txData via performData, controlling the swap routing. MEV bots will systematically sandwich every order execution, extracting the maximum value allowed by slippage settings. Source: performData calldata from any address. Sink: target.call(txData). Missing sanitizer: no msg.sender check, no txData commitment.

findings.title: StopLimit performUpkeep: Permissionless and Bypasses Master
findings.description: Identical access control issue as Bracket.performUpkeep but on StopLimit. Additionally, StopLimit.performUpkeep can be called directly, bypassing AutomationMaster entirely. Any caller can supply attacker-controlled target and txData, enabling systematic MEV extraction on all swapOnFill orders.

findings.title: Systematic MEV Extraction via Permissionless performUpkeep
findings.description: Since Bracket.performUpkeep is permissionless and the caller controls routing, MEV bots will sandwich every order fill. The attacker can submit a transaction with optimal sandwich parameters immediately before and after the order execution, extracting up to the full slippage tolerance. This is guaranteed value extraction, not theoretical, and applies to cumulative slippage of all orders.

findings.title: Oracle Price Used for Both Trigger AND Slippage Protection
findings.description: checkInRange() and getMinAmountReceived() both call MASTER.getExchangeRate() which reads the same oracle. If the oracle is wrong (stale or manipulated), both the trigger condition and slippage floor are compromised simultaneously. An attacker can manipulate one oracle to both trigger the order and reduce its slippage protection, enabling 100% extraction of order value.

findings.title: StopLimit performUpkeep Lacks Access Control
findings.description: Same permissionless execution pattern as Bracket.performUpkeep applied to StopLimit. Direct calls bypass AutomationMaster, enabling MEV on all swapOnFill orders. Any address can call performUpkeep with attacker-controlled routing data.

findings.title: OracleLess fillOrder Enables Systematic MEV
findings.description: fillOrder() is fully permissionless. The filler chooses target and txData. Orders are publicly visible in mempool and on-chain. MEV bots will fill every order at exactly minAmountOut, capturing the full spread between market rate and minAmountOut. Maximum economic impact is (market_rate - minAmountOut) on every executed order.

findings.title: OracleRelay: No Staleness or Round Completeness Checks
findings.description: OracleRelay.currentValue() uses the deprecated latestAnswer() without checking staleness, round completeness, or L2 sequencer uptime. During oracle downtime or delayed round completion, stale prices are returned without any indication. Attackers can exploit orders triggered or protected by stale prices during oracle downtime.

findings.title: TokenEthRelay: Integer Division Before Multiplication Truncates to Zero
findings.description: In TokenEthRelay.currentValue(), the computation uint256(latest) / ethPrice * 1e5 performs division before multiplication. For any token priced below 1 ETH, integer division truncates to zero. This effectively makes the oracle return 0 for most tokens, causing all orders using this oracle to execute against incorrect prices or revert.

findings.title: UniV3TickTwapOracle: Returns Raw Tick Value Instead of Price
findings.description: UniV3TickTwapOracle.currentValue() returns uint256(uint24(tick)) - a raw Uniswap V3 tick value, not a USD price in 1e8 format as the oracle interface expects. All exchange rate calculations using this oracle produce fundamentally incorrect values, as ticks are logarithmic price indices, not actual prices.

findings.title: PythOracle Ignores Pyth Price Exponent Field
findings.description: Pyth prices are represented as price * 10^expo. PythOracle.currentValue() uses the price mantissa but ignores the exponent field entirely. For feeds with non-standard exponents (any expo != -8), the returned price is off by orders of magnitude. This silently corrupts prices for all non-standard Pyth feeds.

findings.title: UniV3TickTwapOracle: TWAP Manipulation and Negative Tick Wrapping
findings.description: UniV3TickTwapOracle has two compounding issues: (1) No minimum lookback enforcement allows flash-loan TWAP manipulation with short observation windows; (2) Negative ticks (valid for pairs where token0 > token1 in price) cast to uint24 wrap to large positive values, producing wildly incorrect prices. Both issues independently lead to corrupted price data.

findings.title: TokenEthRelay: No Staleness or Round Completeness Checks
findings.description: TokenEthRelay.currentValue() uses the deprecated tokenFeed.latestAnswer() without checking staleness, round completeness, or sequencer uptime. Additionally, if the ethOracle is also an OracleRelay instance, both price feeds in the computation lack staleness protection. Combined with VULN-033 (division order bug), TokenEthRelay has two independent high-severity issues affecting price correctness.

findings.title: Bracket modifyOrder: Single-Transaction Recipient Change Enables Phishing
findings.description: Any order owner can change the recipient address in a single transaction via modifyOrder. A phishing attack can trick users into signing a modifyOrder transaction that sets the recipient to an attacker-controlled address. The next order execution then sends funds directly to the attacker. A two-step transfer pattern (propose + confirm from new address) would eliminate this attack vector.

findings.title: StopLimit modifyOrder: Single-Transaction Recipient Hijacking
findings.description: Same phishing vulnerability as Bracket.modifyOrder. StopLimit allows changing the order recipient in one transaction, enabling phishing attacks that redirect order proceeds to an attacker address before the next order execution.

findings.title: StopLimit: Fee-on-Transfer Tokens Break Order Accounting
findings.description: StopLimit.procureTokens() records amountIn as the nominal transfer amount, but fee-on-transfer (FOT) tokens deliver fewer tokens than requested. The stored amountIn exceeds actual tokens held, causing order execution to attempt swapping tokens it does not own. This can cause fund lock or enable cross-order drainage where one order's execution consumes another order's collateral.

findings.title: OracleLess modifyOrder: Single-Transaction Recipient Hijacking
findings.description: Same phishing vulnerability as Bracket.modifyOrder. OracleLess allows changing the order recipient in one transaction, enabling phishing attacks that redirect order proceeds to an attacker address before the next order fill.

findings.title: OracleLess: Fee-on-Transfer Token Accounting Error
findings.description: OracleLess order creation records amountIn as the nominal transfer amount, but FOT tokens deliver fewer tokens. Same vulnerability pattern as StopLimit. Recorded amountIn exceeds actual balance, causing execution failures or cross-order drainage.

findings.title: Front-Running OracleLess Order Creation
findings.description: OracleLess orders are visible in the mempool when submitted. MEV bots can observe the pending createOrder transaction and immediately queue a fillOrder that executes at exactly minAmountOut before the creator's transaction even confirms. This guarantees MEV extraction of the full spread between market price and minAmountOut on every new order.

findings.title: Gas DoS via Large Token Whitelist in OracleLess
findings.description: OracleLess.verifyTokenBalances() iterates over all whitelisted tokens on every fillOrder call. If the whitelist grows large, fillOrder becomes prohibitively gas expensive and effectively disabled. An attacker or admin error adding many tokens could permanently DoS order execution.

findings.title: AutomationMaster: XOR Toggle Pattern for safeTargets is Error-Prone
findings.description: AutomationMaster uses safeTargets[targets[i]] = !safeTargets[targets[i]] to manage the whitelist. Calling the toggle function twice for the same address accidentally re-enables it. An operator error or race condition can inadvertently whitelist or delist targets. Should use separate addSafeTarget/removeSafeTarget functions with explicit bool parameters.

findings.title: AutomationMaster performUpkeep: Permissionless Routing to Sub-Keepers
findings.description: AutomationMaster.performUpkeep() routes execution to sub-keepers (Bracket, StopLimit) without any access control on the master level. This is a duplicate of the individual contract vulnerabilities at the master orchestration layer, confirming there is no defense-in-depth. Any caller can route arbitrary performUpkeep calls.

findings.title: feeBips = 10000 Causes Division by Zero in getMinAmountReceivedAfterFee
findings.description: Both Bracket and OracleLess allow feeBips up to 10000 (check is feeBips <= 10000). getMinAmountReceivedAfterFee() computes (minAmountOut * 10000) / (10000 - feeBips), which causes division by zero when feeBips = 10000. Any order with this fee value permanently reverts on execution, locking user funds in the contract until cancelled.

findings.title: Bracket: Fee-on-Transfer Tokens Break Order Accounting
findings.description: Bracket.procureTokens() / _createOrder() records the nominal amountIn but FOT tokens deliver fewer tokens. The stored amountIn exceeds actual balance held, causing execution failures or cross-order drainage. Same vulnerability pattern as StopLimit (VULN-014) and OracleLess (VULN-023).

findings.title: Excess ETH Not Refunded in StopLimit paysFee
findings.description: StopLimit uses msg.value >= orderFee to accept payment but only forwards orderFee to the automation system. Any excess ETH sent by the user is permanently locked in the contract. Users who overpay by mistake cannot recover the difference.

findings.title: Excess ETH Not Refunded in OracleLess paysFee
findings.description: Same excess ETH locking issue as StopLimit. OracleLess accepts msg.value >= orderFee but only uses orderFee, permanently locking any excess ETH sent by the user.

findings.title: StopLimit Direction Set from Potentially Manipulated Oracle at Creation
findings.description: The direction field in StopLimit orders is permanently set at creation time based on getExchangeRate() > stopLimitPrice. If the oracle is manipulated at creation time (e.g., via TWAP manipulation), direction is set incorrectly, causing the order to trigger on the wrong price movement. Limited to a griefing attack - the user can cancel and recreate the order.

findings.title: Malicious Whitelisted Target Can Steal Approved Tokens
findings.description: OracleLess allows order execution to call any safeTarget with arbitrary calldata. A malicious or compromised whitelisted target contract could transfer tokens that have approval to the OracleLess contract. Impact depends on the governance process and trust model for the safeTargets whitelist. Requires human review to assess operational risk.

findings.title: modifyOrder Pulls Tokens from Old Recipient After Recipient Change
findings.description: When modifyOrder is called to change both the recipient and increase amountIn, additional tokens are pulled from the original recipient rather than the new recipient or the order owner. This may be an intentional design choice or a latent accounting bug. Requires human review to confirm intended behavior.

findings.title: No slippageBips Bounds Check in getMinAmountReceived
findings.description: getMinAmountReceived() does not validate that slippageBips is within a safe range. If slippageBips is set to an extreme value (e.g., > 10000), it could underflow or produce zero slippage protection. Whether callers always validate this before calling requires human review of all call sites.
